evidence_quotes.quote: Cross-sectional household surveys were conducted in 2016 and 2017 in 17 sub-districts of two governorates
During the survey, household water was tested for free chlorine residual (FCR).
Households spent ~ 20% of income on water and reported market-available hygiene items were unaffordable.

rationale: This observational study analyzes repeated cross-sectional household WASH surveys (2016, n=1,281; 2017, n=1,360) and household drinking-water testing in opposition-controlled southern Syria using two-sample t-tests and mixed-effects logistic regressions. Empirically, the study tests technical/operational humanitarian Water Safety Plan (WSP) programming (chlorination training, chlorine and tester distribution, chlorination stations, pipe/pump repairs, and volunteer awareness campaigns) alongside physical/behavioral WASH covariates and wartime water-source shifts (piped network vs. private water trucking due to conflict-induced power and infrastructure breakdown), rather than testing any formal legal, regulatory, tariff, or ownership rule (NONE_NO_RULE_MECHANISM; targeted subsidies/vouchers and market regulation are proposed only as policy recommendations in the Discussion). Across the 2016-2017 comparisons, multiple WASH access outcomes are co-centrally evaluated—drinking-water safety (FCR > 0.1 mg/L, the sole WASH outcome modeled as a regression dependent variable), water quantity/continuity/functional sanitation (effective_access), piped network coverage on premises (primary_connection), and household income share spent on water and hygiene affordability (economic_access)—making effective_access the primary outcome family and multiple the multi-outcome label.
